Package org.aeonbits.owner.util.bytesize

Class ByteSize

java.lang.Object
org.aeonbits.owner.util.bytesize.ByteSize
All Implemented Interfaces:
Serializable, Comparable<ByteSize>
public final class ByteSize extends Object implements Comparable<ByteSize>, Serializable
A unit of byte size, such as "512 kilobytes". This class models a two part byte count size, one part being a value and the other part being a ByteSizeUnit. This class supports converting to another ByteSizeUnit.

Instances are immutable, and the class is final: equals(Object) compares the number of bytes across units, a statement that a subclass adding a field of its own could not honour.

Instances are ordered by the number of bytes they represent, consistently with equals(Object).

Instances are Serializable, and serialization preserves the unit the size was written in along with the value, so what comes back reads the same way as what went in.

Author:
Stefan Freyr Stefansson

    • getBytes

      public BigInteger getBytes()
      Returns the number of bytes that this byte size represents after multiplying the unit factor with the value. Since the value part can be a represented by a decimal, there is some possibility of a rounding error. Therefore, the result of multiplying the value and the unit factor are always rounded towards positive infinity to the nearest integer value (see RoundingMode.CEILING) to make sure that this method never gives values that are too small.
      Returns:
      number of bytes this byte size represents after factoring in the unit.

    • convertTo

      public ByteSize convertTo(ByteSizeUnit unit)
      Creates a new ByteSize representing the same byte size but in a different unit. Scale of the value (number of decimal points) is handled automatically but if a non-terminating decimal expansion occurs, an ArithmeticException is thrown.

      The conversion changes nothing but the unit: what comes back equals(Object) what went in, in every unit and for every value. It used to round the byte count towards positive infinity first, the way getBytes() does, which turned 1.5 B into 2 B — a conversion that reports a size other than the one it was given, and it did so even when the unit asked for was the one the size was already written in. The rounding belongs to getBytes(), whose caller wants a whole number of bytes; it does not belong here.

      Parameters:
      unit - the unit for the new ByteSize.
      Returns:
      a new ByteSize instance representing the same byte size as this but using the specified unit.
      Throws:
      ArithmeticException - if a non-terminating decimal expansion occurs during calculation.

    • in

      public ByteSize in(ByteSizeStandard standard)
      Returns the same byte size expressed in the unit of the given standard that makes it readable: the largest one in which the value does not fall below one, so that 2048576 bytes read as 2.048576 MB in ByteSizeStandard.SI and as 1.95367431640625 MiB in ByteSizeStandard.IEC.

      Where convertTo(ByteSizeUnit) needs to be told the unit, this method needs only the family of units to pick from, which is what one usually has: a size read from a configuration file is to be logged or shown, and the unit that suits it depends on how large it turned out to be.

      The result is canonical: two sizes that are equal give the same answer, whatever unit each of them was written in, so 1 MB and 1000000 B both read as 1 MB in SI. That is what makes this the natural way to display the outcome of a calculation, where the unit of the operands is an accident of how they were written.

      The conversion is exact: every factor is a power of 1000 or of 1024, neither of which has a prime factor beyond 2 and 5, so no division involved here can fail to terminate. A size below one byte, or zero, reads in bytes, there being no larger unit that fits; a negative size keeps its sign and takes the unit its magnitude asks for.

      Parameters:
      standard - the family of units to express this size in.
      Returns:
      an equal byte size, written in the unit of that standard that suits it.
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if the standard is null.
      Since:
      2.0.0

    • compareTo

      public int compareTo(ByteSize other)
      Compares two byte sizes by the amount of data they represent, so that 1 MiB comes after 1 MB and the unit each of them is written in does not enter into it.

      The ordering is consistent with equals: this method returns zero exactly when equals(Object) returns true. That is what makes a TreeSet of byte sizes agree with a HashSet of the same sizes on which of them are duplicates.

      Specified by:
      compareTo in interface Comparable<ByteSize>
      Parameters:
      other - the byte size to compare this one with.
      Returns:
      a negative integer, zero, or a positive integer as this size is smaller than, equal to, or larger than the given one.
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if the given byte size is null.
      Since:
      2.0.0

    • hashCode

      public int hashCode()
      Derived from the same number of bytes equals(Object) compares, and from nothing else: two sizes that are equal because they are the same amount written in different units, or with a different number of decimals, have to agree on the hash code as well, or the type does not work as a key of a HashMap nor as an element of a HashSet.

      The trailing zeros are stripped first because that is exactly what BigDecimal.equals(Object) counts and BigDecimal.compareTo(BigDecimal) does not: 1000 and 1.000E+3 are the same size written twice, and they have to hash alike.
